title: Photochemical Events and Diversity of Eubacterial Photosensors
content: Photosensory proteins enable bacteria to perceive and respond to changes in their environment by converting photon absorption into biochemical signals. Despite their structural and functional diversity, they share the ability to couple primary photochemical events to conformational changes that trigger signaling cascades and regulate biological activity. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying photoactivation in seven families of eubacterial photosensors: photoactive yellow proteins (PYP), Cobalamin-binding (B12) photosensors, Orange carotenoid proteins (OCP), light–oxygen–voltage (LOV) proteins, blue-light using FAD (BLUF) proteins, bacteriophytochromes (BphP), cyanobacteriochromes (CBCR), cryptochromes (CRY) and sensory rhodopsins (SR). The manuscript focuses on the nature of the chromophores, their excited-state dynamics, and the primary photochemical events, including photoisomerisation, covalent bond formation and cleavage, and electron- and proton-transfer processes. The recent advances in ultrafast spectroscopy, time-resolved structural methods, and computational approaches have provided detailed insights into transient intermediates. By comparing these distinct photosensor families, this review highlights both the diversity of light-triggered molecular transformations and the common principles governing the conversion of photoexcitation into biological signals. The emerging picture underscores the active role of the protein matrix in controlling reaction pathways, photochemical efficiency, and signaling dynamics.
